items.title: DuoCook: An Overcooked-Inspired Benchmark for Visual Planning and Coordination
items.summary: Coordinating two players in a cooking task requires a vision-language agent to track changing scene states, sequence recipe steps, and allocate shared resources under a time budget. We introduce an Overcooked-inspired benchmark for evaluating these capabilities in Unreal Engine environments constructed using coding agents. A single vision-language model controls both players from top-down visual observations, selecting high-level actions while the engine executes navigation. The benchmark contains 20 maps in five categories. These categories support evaluation of centralized coordination under equipment contention, changing terrain, and handoff dependencies. A prop legend and pot ingredient-count indicators provide explicit visual cues, while grid-based destinations support spatial grounding. The evaluation compares four VLMs on all 20 maps, measuring task score, order completion, delivery precision, action acceptance rate, and model API expenditure. A memory ablation on the same 20 maps examines the effect of a shared, self-authored notebook while retaining six-response action history in both conditions. The strongest evaluated model, \texttt{gpt-6-astra}, achieves 26.2\% mean order completion. Notebook memory has mixed score effects across models, with positive mean differences for Claude and Qwen and negative differences for GPT and Gemini.

items.title: Evaluating the Applicability of LLM Inference Optimizations on Apple Silicon
items.summary: Apple Silicon is among the most widely used platforms for local LLM inference, yet nearly all inference optimizations are designed and validated on server-class NVIDIA GPUs under batched serving workloads. Which optimizations retain their benefits when moved to Apple Silicon, and what determines their applicability? We evaluate four optimization families: KV-cache pruning, speculative decoding, ported GPU kernels, and post-training quantization. Experiments span four Apple machines under a common single-request decode workload, with matched RTX 4090 comparisons where possible. KV-cache pruning can reach up to 1.75 times end-to-end throughput on Apple but can reduce throughput on desktop NVIDIA GPUs. Under the common benchmark, all evaluated speculative decoding methods reduce throughput on Apple, despite reported 2-6 times gains on server GPUs. CUDA kernel designs transfer only partially: public Metal lacks asynchronous copy, and batch-one decode makes several serving-oriented mechanisms inapplicable, although transferable components yield up to 1.20 times decode throughput. Quantization gains vary by machine. Across four families, a reported speedup is not a portable property of a technique alone but a joint function of technique, runtime, hardware contract, and workload regime.

items.title: If you are building AI for finance, get out while you can
items.summary: LLMs are good with probabilistic logic (words), but not as good with deterministic logic (numbers). As oppose to what everybody thought 3 years ago, LLMs are not very good with finance. Makes sense when you think about it as AI in 2025 still rely heavily on language transformers, and transformers are more or less probability calculators. Ai agents in accounting firms are way less effective than Ai agents in law firms for example. 1 wrong word in the bylaws can break your entire company. Accounting is more precise, it tolerates less mistakes, and the rules that govern it are much less option to intrepretation. In accounting, the rules are more grounded. Not in precedent but in a generally accepted specific rulebook. Gross profits mean the same in the US as it does in Bangladesh, and it will mean the same 100 years in the future. In accounting, probability is very bad. A single bad journal entry in a 100,000 ledger can distort the entire balance sheet. And we know that no LLM will ever reach 100% accuracy rate because its reasoning is probabilistic, not absolute. Campfire raised $65m and built an entire accounting module from scratch, they only managed to achieve ~95% accuracy rate. It might feel like 95% is very close to 100%, but that is not how it works. A football player such as Arbeloa, who ranks in the 80th percentile, is not remotely comparable to someone in the 90th percentile. Now imagine a player who is better than 99% of all football players who ever lived; that superstar is on an entirely different level, and Arbeloa would lose 0–10 to him every single time. All of which without mentioning the 99.99th percentile, where the gap becomes unimaginable to human minds. Accounting follows the same power law; 99% accuracy rate might sound close to perfect, but across 100k ledger entries, that means ~1k bad entires. You can hire someone to go through the bad ones, but how can we know which ones are going to be bad. Its definitly a cost saver, but it's not the same as coding or legal. Also, all the major labs are going after accounting after they finish with coding, so margins are going down fast. Yes, most accountants have an accuracy rate below 90%, but humans are allowed to make mistakes because YOU CAN SUE A HUMAN. That might not be a big deal in other areas, but when it comes to finance, companies suddenly get very risk averse. Its not even the hullication part that scares them, but the part where the Ai missed something. Bookkeeping can be divided into smaller tasks and automated fine, but accounting is a different story. Its about accountibility more than anything else. Humans have a MAJOR advantage over AI; we can be held legally accountable. If it weren't for that, most of us will be obsolete already. Under Sarbanes Oxley, any company no matter how small must have a "human" finance officer (CFO), and a "human" controller. Courts won't allow an Ai attorney to present a case no matter how good it was at the job.

The reports are sent without human review, and project maintainers can choose to validate their findings and decide which proposed fixes to accept.

items.title: Social-HUMINT: An LLM-Augmented Unified Framework for Measuring Social Media Exposure
items.summary:
In the post-API landscape, social-media profiling has become inexpensive and automated: Large Language Models (LLMs) can extract structured information from unstructured content and deduce attributes users never disclosed. A person's true exposure is not what they post but what can be inferred from it. As these practices become routine, exposure to social engineering attacks becomes an operational certainty, demanding a shared framework for assessment and mitigation.
  We make this exposure measurable by quantifying how accurately a target can be profiled, and how far that profile enables social engineering attacks. Because no existing model fully spans this continuum, we unify Social Media Intelligence (SOCMINT) and Cyber Human Intelligence (Cyber-HUMINT), two individual-focused disciplines that evolved separately, into a single doctrine-grounded taxonomy of 38 capabilities across the Cyber Threat Intelligence lifecycle, where user profiling bridges passive collection and active engagement. Domain experts validated the taxonomy (Fleiss' $κ$ = 0.92).
  We operationalize its core path (extraction, inference, and susceptibility assessment) as an LLM-augmented multi-agent pipeline, evaluated on real participants' public data. Susceptibility is assessed indirectly: the pipeline predicts how each target would rank personalized engagement options, matching their actual choices significantly above chance. This ranking capacity captures the personalization on which tailored attacks depend. The underlying profiles are accurate: extraction reaches F1 = 97.3%, and inferred attributes score 4.73/5, both far above rule-based and NER-based baselines at negligible cost. The framework augments security analysts' tradecraft rather than replacing it and enables defenders to gauge their own exposure before an adversary does.

items.title: Study Finds AI-generated Code Fails to Boost Productivity Due to Downstream Bottlenecks
items.summary:
A recent Harvard study of 718 firms, using the Jellyfish analytics platform, finds that although AI coding assistants and agents increase code volume, this does not translate into a corresponding increase in completed work, partly because AI-generated code increases the workload in later stages of development, particularly code review.

By Sergio De Simone

items.title: claude-code v2.1.309
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Fixed sandboxed Bash commands on macOS and Linux running the shell's startup files outside the sandbox before each command
  • Fixed macOS sandbox denyWrite glob patterns not applying at a path's real location when the pattern's folder is reached through a symlink
  • Fixed sandboxed commands and auto-accepted edits being able to modify the MCP config file passed with --mcp-config
  • Fixed a disabled MCP server being reconnected by a later permission prompt in print and SDK sessions
  • Fixed the Bash permission check trusting a variable set by a command whose redirect can fail to open
  • Fixed Bash permission checks not prompting for some compound commands that change directory before running git when the cd is wrapped or prefixed, as they do for a plain cd
  • Fixed an Edit(path) deny rule not blocking a Bash redirect to that path in some commands that also held a subshell
  • Fixed worktree-isolated sessions accepting some locale-prefixed commands the isolation guard should refuse
  • Fixed worktree-isolated sessions on zsh accepting some arithmetic commands that the isolation guard should refuse
  • Fixed worktrees and branch checkouts that Claude Code creates so they ignore git replace refs, as its other git operations already do
  • Fixed profile store write protection not applying when the config directory is reached through a symlink
  • Fixed sessions compacting repeatedly after reading files under a very large nested CLAUDE.md; a nested CLAUDE.md over the size limit now loads only its start
  • Fixed ctrl+enter (send now) only queuing a message when pressed before the response had started, and restarting a prompt's hooks while leaving the message queued when pressed while those hooks were running
  • Fixed key-bound slash commands running in the shell from ! mode
  • Fixed ctrl+o not showing messages from other agents and sessions that are still waiting to be delivered; they now appear in full under the transcript, marked as waiting
  • Fixed long tool output previews being cut through an emoji, leaving session transcripts that jq could not parse
  • Fixed Read reporting "File does not exist" for PDF page ranges in Linux sandboxes that share the parent's /proc
  • Fixed messages from a Claude Desktop-hosted session sometimes being lost when its connection refreshed
  • Fixed features missing from Claude Code sessions in the Claude desktop app when the terminal on the same computer was signed in to a different account or organization
  • Fixed the claude remote-control status line showing HEAD as the branch for a folder that is not in a git repository
  • Fixed split-pane agent teammates not inheriting the tool deny and --tools rules given on the leader's command line
  • Fixed sessions renamed with /rename appearing to other sessions under a generated name after a VS Code window reload or a non-interactive --resume
  • Fixed the /rewind list showing "No code changes" for a turn that changed checkpointed files through /code-review --fix, a subagent or a shell command
  • Fixed /privacy-settings showing an out-of-date "Help improve our AI models" value; it now also says when the setting can't be fetched
  • Fixed feedback saying "try again later" when your organization does not accept feedback; it now shows the server's reason and where to report a bug
  • Fixed oversized /feedback reports failing instead of being resent without the transcript
  • Fixed a skill in an --add-dir folder being unreachable when another skill already held its name; it is now offered as <folder>:<name>
  • Fixed /verify and /code-review not finding a nested package's own skill when its files were changed from the shell
  • Fixed the /claude-api skill saying that ant beta:worker poll --on-work passes trace context to the command
  • Fixed the /claude-api skill's C# tracing setup missing spans from the cloud platform clients
  • Fixed the /claude-api skill saying that API spans for requests to Claude Platform on AWS can't join the caller's trace
  • Fixed hooks that run in PowerShell not blocking when the hook's program exits with code 2, and on Windows PreToolUse and PermissionRequest hooks with "shell": "powershell" failing open when Git for Windows isn't installed
  • Fixed a mod's turn.step hook that names a model by alias, such as haiku, failing every request with a model error: the alias now resolves to its model
  • Fixed plugins and skills synced from claude.ai being removed, sometimes mid-session, after a disk read error
  • Fixed artifact publishes and updates being refused for some ordinary pages, such as pages with certain minified scripts or artifacts Claude could not read first
  • Fixed Claude asking for permission on each artifact update for the rest of a turn after the conversation was compacted in that turn
  • Fixed fine-grained tool streaming staying off on Amazon Bedrock when ANTHROPIC_BEDROCK_BASE_URL is set to the default bedrock-runtime.<region>.amazonaws.com endpoint
  • Fixed the "Waiting for API response" hint flickering behind gateways that send only keepalive pings: routes off Anthropic's backend now wait 45 seconds
  • Fixed Claude notifying unrelated GitHub users by writing role names and placeholders as mentions in PRs, issues and comments
  • Linux: Fixed sandbox write denies lifting when a background command outlived the session
  • Windows: Fixed PowerShell permission checks auto-approving some Set-Location or cd commands that target the current directory and carry extra arguments; these now prompt for approval
  • macOS: Fixed the "Install Command Line Developer Tools" dialog opening each time Claude Code starts on a Mac without Xcode or the Command Line Tools
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed --startup-timeout-min stopping a session whose first prompt, such as /code-review, was still working in a subagent; a frozen process is still stopped
  • Improved the speed of many git commands Claude Code runs for itself on Windows; on every platform, errors from those commands now show in English even when git is set to another language
  • Improved the error when a hooks module is nested too deep to load: it now names the file instead of showing a bare stack-overflow message
  • Improved disk-full handling: a Bash command cut off by a full disk now says so and names the folder to free up, and starting on a full temp volume prints a clear message, not a raw ENOSPC error
  • Improved the /claude-api skill to offer API tracing alongside SDK tracing when asked to add OpenTelemetry
  • Improved the /claude-api skill to check the live docs before saying a feature is unsupported
  • Self-hosted runner: Improved sessions that move to a new runner: Claude now sees the tool call that was interrupted, marked as outcome unknown
  • Updated the bundled dataviz skill to accept APCA as a text-contrast measure (keeping WCAG 2 ratios where AA conformance is required), add an apca(text, background) function to its palette validator scripts, and say whether a label inside a colored chart fill should be white or near-black
  • Updated the /claude-api skill: service account keys and Workload Identity Federation tokens can now manage OpenTelemetry destinations
  • Changed sed -i to get the standard Bash prompt and run as written, not a simulated file-edit preview; like other Bash edits, it is no longer restored by /rewind

  • Changed commands the settings exclude from the sandbox to ask before writing to its write-list paths while the sandbox is enabled but cannot run; the unsandboxed fallback is refused there

  • [VSCode] Fixed Ctrl+J in the chat input always inserting a newline: it is now left to VS Code and the OS when "ctrl+j" is set to null in the Chat context of ~/.claude/keybindings.json
  • [VSCode] Fixed a mod's "From the … plugin" label above the prompt being drawn over the slash command and @-mention menus (#102981)
  • [VSCode] Fixed an empty list item, paragraph or code block, and list items renumbered from 1, when pasting copied LaTeX math

  • [VSCode] Improved Edit and Write speed in the chat panel: the wait for new problems after each edit is now 0.75 seconds in most cases, down from 1 to 1.5 seconds

  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed the cloud environment editor shuffling environment variables and adding backslashes to values that contain both kinds of quote
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed the self-hosted environment details dialog in admin settings so its title, tabs and buttons stay in view while only the content scrolls
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed the "read documentation" tool row in cloud sessions, which showed escaped JSON instead of a readable page
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved a cloud session's Changes pane, which now says when it lists only pushed commits or only Claude's edits

  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude ignoring untagged messages in a Slack channel after its workspace moved to a different Claude organization, including unshared channels on Enterprise Grid

items.title: On the Token Collapse Phenomenon in Textual Graph Soft Prompting
items.summary: Recent methods for injecting graph structure into LLM prompts include graph soft prompting, in which a graph neural network (GNN) learns graph-specific tokens that capture relational information among entities in textual prompts. G-Retriever combines graph soft prompts with a verbalized description of the same graph to strengthen the textual prompt signal. We conduct an in-depth analysis of G-Retriever and uncover a pathological behavior we term token collapse. Across three benchmarks, three graph encoders, two LLM families, and both frozen and LoRA-adapted models, G-Retriever's graph tokens become almost indistinguishable across inputs. We provide evidence that the same failure is inherited by subsequent methods, even with multi-token pooling. Under the standard setup, swapping a token with the dataset mean, a token from another example, or one derived from a corrupted graph produces no resolved answer-level effect in accuracy. Moreover, a learned constant prompt that never accesses the graph matches or surpasses G-Retriever on all three benchmarks. These findings indicate that, rather than conveying graph content as intended, the collapsed token functions primarily as a generic soft prompt. We also examine conditions linked to this collapse and propose a two-stage procedure that yields non-collapsed tokens while maintaining competitive performance in most cases. However, token variability alone does not prove that the model uses graph information: via interventions and decoding probes, we show that depending on the configuration, a token can reflect the question, an answer prior, or graph-derived content that the LLM may or may not use. Overall, our results offer a practical approach to evaluating graph-token alignment rather than inferring it from task accuracy alone. Code to reproduce our experiments is available at https://github.com/difra100/Token_Collapse_KGQA.
